sample.task:
Give and explain five insights you gained into education system in Ireland. Refer to the following article in your answer and support it with quotes from the article. There are many ingredients boiling in the pot of Irish higher education and the broth looks far from satisfying. As students begin or return to college, a now familiar range of challenges are listed: accommodation, commuting, student “charges”, under-investment and anxiety. Academics are also concerned about the threat of artificial intelligence (AI) and our research culture, as well as the ongoing impact of grade inflation.
For all the venting of these issues, they are not often assessed through the framework of a proper educational philosophy. When Niamh Bhreathnach, the Labour minister for education from 1993-97 died earlier this year, her obituaries noted that on taking office, when she questioned the philosophy underpinning the work of her department, the response from some civil servants was “we don’t do philosophy”.
Such dismissiveness was countered with constant references to aspirations for a “world class” education system and research culture. Reimagining third-level education led to greater State intervention and investment. Expenditure per student increased by 54 per cent in the late 1990s; student numbers in publicly funded higher education institutes increased from 107,950 in 1992-93 to 222,618 from 2015-16.
The changes, however, were too often interrupted and without proper consultation; in 2015 one sociologist of higher education, Patrick Clancy, suggested the lack of engagement between critics and policymakers reflected “a more widespread failure to develop any serious public and intellectual discourse about higher education policy”.
Between 2007 and 2021, full-time and part-time PhD enrolments rose from 5,989 to 10,013, a rise of 67 per cent. Earlier this year, PhD students protested that their average income, including research, teaching and supervisory work, was €7.88 per hour, far below the minimum wage. An independent review has since recommended they be paid €25,000 a year for their world-class research.
At the same time, almost 2,000 academics signed a letter expressing concerns about the underfunding of third level. With the Government preparing legislation to create a new research and innovation funding agency, they asked for greater consultation with the research community, a proper balance between science, technology, engineering and maths (Stem) and arts, humanities and social sciences, as well as democratic governance and transparent selection of those overseeing the agency. They highlighted that Ireland invests 1.23 per cent of GDP on research development compared with the EU average of 2.32 per cent.
Last year, Minister for Further and Higher Education Simon Harris acknowledged a “core funding gap” of €307 million for higher education but just €40 million was allocated to address this. Third-level student-to-staff ratios have increased from 16:1 in 2007 to 23:1 today, compared with a European average of 15:1.
It is a relief to hear Harris promise the hiring of 1,500 permanent full-time staff as the casualisation of third-level employment has been so damaging. But in tandem, as Pól Ó Dochartaigh, registrar of the University of Galway, asked recently, to what extent are extra university places related to “structured planning” and a “reflection on what society as a whole needs”? A serious discussion, he argues, “about the over-arching strategic role of third-level education and the rates of participation in it is long overdue in the interests of the country, and of the students themselves”.
And how are to we measure the extent of student talent? Inflated Leaving Certificate grades are perpetuating unreal expectations, overestimating student ability and adding to anxiety. It requires a courageous minister for education to put a halt to it.
A recent OECD report on this matter asserted: “Unabated, this type of grade inflation will . . . undermine stakeholder confidence in the system as a whole . . . Considering how to ensure that grade inflation is controlled for future generations taking the Leaving Certificate will be important for the assessment’s integrity and to discriminate between different levels of achievement.”
Increased drop-out rates, complications for those from other jurisdictions wishing to study here and students being unable to access courses they are qualified for are just some of the consequences. Between 5 and 6 per cent of Leaving Cert grades were H1s before the pandemic, which increased to more than 14 per cent from 2021 to 2023. A total of 1,100 students achieved the maximum 625 points in 2022, compared with just 200 in 2019.
Nor are universities immune from this practice. It is thoroughly justifiable to look askance at the number of first-class honours degrees in recent years and wonder how many of them are really of that standard: 23.5 per cent of graduates were awarded first-class degrees in 2022 compared with 15.9 in 2015.
Third-level educators are swamped with managerial directives and bureaucracy relating to teaching and learning obligations. But students also need to embrace their own code of behaviour, recognising that the use of AI for the purpose of generating assignment answers is cheating, undermines their own intellectual autonomy and the idea of a university. There is an onus on them too to philosophise on educational matters.

sample.rejected:
1. **Increased State Intervention and Investment**: The article highlights a significant increase in state intervention and investment in Irish higher education, with expenditure per student rising by 54% in the late 1990s and student numbers in publicly funded higher education institutes increasing from 107,950 in 1992-93 to 222,618 from 2015-16. This suggests a commitment to expanding access to higher education and improving the quality of education through increased funding.

2. **Challenges and Concerns in Higher Education**: Despite the increased investment, the article points out that there are numerous challenges facing Irish higher education, including accommodation issues, commuting difficulties, student charges, under-investment, anxiety, the threat of artificial intelligence (AI), grade inflation, and the ongoing impact of grade inflation. These challenges indicate that while there has been progress, there are still significant issues that need to be addressed to ensure the quality and accessibility of higher education.

3. **Lack of Public and Intellectual Discourse**: The article mentions that there has been a lack of engagement between critics and policymakers, reflecting a "more widespread failure to develop any serious public and intellectual discourse about higher education policy." This suggests that while there has been increased investment and intervention, there is a need for more open and inclusive discussions about the direction and priorities of higher education policy.

4. **Underfunding and Staffing Issues**: The article highlights concerns about the underfunding of third-level education, with Ireland investing 1.23% of GDP on research development compared to the EU average of 2.32%. It also mentions a "core funding gap" of €307 million for higher education, with only €40 million allocated to address this. Additionally, the article points out the casualisation of third-level employment and the increasing student-to-staff ratios, indicating that there are significant staffing and funding challenges in Irish higher education.

5. **Grade Inflation and Its Consequences**: The article discusses the issue of grade inflation, with unabated grade inflation undermining stakeholder confidence in the system and complicating the assessment of student achievement. It also mentions the increased drop-out rates and the challenges faced by students from other jurisdictions wishing to study in Ireland. This suggests that grade inflation is a significant issue that needs to be addressed to ensure the integrity and fairness of the higher education system.

6. **The Role of AI and Student Behaviour**: The article mentions concerns about the threat of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education and the need for students to embrace their own code of behaviour, recognizing that the use of AI for the purpose of generating assignment answers is cheating. This highlights the need for students to develop their own intellectual autonomy and for educators to consider the implications of AI in higher education.

In summary, the article provides insights into the challenges and opportunities in Irish higher education, highlighting the need for increased investment, open and inclusive discussions about policy, addressing underfunding and staffing issues, tackling grade inflation, and considering the implications of AI. These insights suggest that while there has been progress in expanding access to higher education, there are still significant challenges that need to be addressed to ensure the quality and accessibility of education in Ireland.

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 每一个洞察项下都明确标注了“Quote:”并引用了原文中的一段话作为支撑，每条都至少包含一条直接引语。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 并非每一条洞察都包含直接引语。例如，第1条（关于国家干预和支出增加）、第2条（列举挑战）和第4条（关于GDP投入和学生与教职员工比例）均未引用原文中的任何直接引语，仅使用了间接陈述或数据概括。只有第3条和第5条包含了直接引语。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 所引用的片段与对应的洞察在语义上高度相关：第一条引用佐证了缺乏哲学的态度；第二条引用支持了投资增加的论点；第三条引用虽侧重治理结构，但也属于对资金和人员问题的背景描述（学术界要求透明度和咨询）；第四条引用直接对应成绩膨胀的数据；第五条引用直接支持了对战略角色的讨论需求。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 由于部分条目（如第1、2、4条）根本没有包含直接引语，因此无法满足“所引用的片段与洞察语义紧密相关并能直接佐证”的要求。对于包含引语的条目（如第3条），引语确实相关，但整体标准因缺失引语的条目而未被满足。

criteria.question: 回答是否明确列出了恰好五个关于爱尔兰教育体系的独特见解？
每个列出的见解是否都附带了清晰的解释或分析，而不仅仅是陈述事实？
每个见解是否都直接引用了提供的文章内容（使用引号或明确的文本指代）来作为支撑证据？
所有五个见解的内容是否均源自提供的文章，未引入文章以外的虚构数据、报告或外部事实？

rubric.analysis: 评分标准设计严格遵循任务核心要求：1. 必须提供恰好五个关于爱尔兰教育体系的见解；2. 每个见解必须包含解释；3. 所有观点必须基于提供的文章并引用原文支持。背景信息（如文章中提到的具体数据、年份、人名）仅作为验证依据，不作为额外输出义务。权重分配上，‘内容数量与相关性’（5个见解且针对爱尔兰教育）占最高权重，确保回答紧扣主题；‘证据支撑’（引用原文）次之，确保观点有据可依；‘解释深度’再次，确保见解有逻辑展开；‘事实准确性’虽重要，但鉴于任务是基于给定文本而非外部事实核查，主要关注是否准确转述文本而非编造外部数据，因此权重适中。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 回答明确列出了恰好五个见解，分别以编号 1 至 5 呈现，涵盖了教育哲学缺失、国家干预增加、资金与人员不足、成绩通胀以及高等教育战略角色讨论缺乏这五个独特方面。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 回答列出了6个见解（编号1至6），而不是任务要求的“恰好五个”。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 每个见解在陈述事实后都附带了分析性解释。例如，见解 1 指出引语表明系统缺乏指导性的教育哲学；见解 4 分析了成绩通胀可能损害系统的完整性和信誉；见解 5 解释了该观点暗示需要重新审视爱尔兰高等教育的目标和目的。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 每个列出的见解都包含了文章中的事实数据，并附带了分析性陈述（如使用'suggests that...'句式）来解释这些数据的含义或影响，不仅仅是单纯的事实罗列。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 每个见解下方都直接引用了文章中的原文（使用双引号或单引号），且引文内容与见解主题紧密相关，如见解 3 引用了关于学术委员会要求咨询和治理的具体段落，见解 4 引用了关于一等学位比例变化的具体数据段落。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 并非所有五个（实际为六个）见解都直接引用了文章内容。例如，第1点、第2点和第4点虽然使用了数据，但并未使用引号（quotes）直接引用原文文本；只有第3点明确使用了引号引用了Patrick Clancy的话。任务要求每个见解都必须有引文支撑。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 所有五个见解及其引用的数据（如支出增长 54%、一等学位比例从 15.9% 增至 23.5% 等）均严格源自提供的文章内容，未引入任何文章以外的虚构数据、外部报告或事实。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 回答中提到的所有数据（如54%支出增长、GDP占比、资金缺口金额、学生人数等）和观点均源自提供的文章，未引入外部虚构数据或事实。
